questions.question: What does MEAL stand for in this framework?

options.text: Measurement, Evidence, Accountability and Leadership
Measurement, Evaluation, Adoption and Learning
Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning
Monitoring, Evidence, Assessment and Learning

questions.explanation: MEAL stands for Monitoring, Evaluation, Accountability and Learning. The framework connects these functions so evidence supports decisions and credible accounts of change.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Read the framework title and the purpose of the new approach.

questions.question: What is the main shift in CIMMYT’s new MEAL approach?

options.text: Measure institutional success mainly through delivery totals.
Connect reported results to traceable observation-level evidence.
Transfer routine monitoring from projects to investors.
Replace field records with a single annual project narrative.

questions.explanation: The new approach connects reported results to records of what changed, for whom and under which conditions. Reporting summaries remain useful when teams can trace them to the evidence.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Compare report-based monitoring with observation-based evidence.

questions.question: Which strategic effect concerns timely insights that inform decisions during implementation?

options.text: Impact
Agility and foresight
Evidence
Collaboration

questions.explanation: Agility and foresight concern high-frequency insights that inform decisions during implementation. The framework lists this alongside evidence, collaboration and impact.
questions.reviewTip: Review the four strategic effects and their stated purposes.

questions.question: A breeding team has trial results while a socioeconomics team has adoption studies. What should MEAL enable?

options.text: Keep each dataset separate and combine only the final project summaries.
Replace the adoption studies with the number of trial locations.
Use the trial results as the complete evidence of farmer adoption.
Connect the evidence to examine the contribution from breeding to farmer outcomes.

questions.explanation: The framework connects breeding, adoption, agronomic and development-project evidence. Linking these sources can support a fuller account of contribution, subject to suitable methods and definitions.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Trace the links between breeding results, adoption and farmer outcomes.

questions.question: Why does the framework say CIMMYT’s MEAL function needs to change?

options.text: Institutional learning should depend on report summaries without source records.
CIMMYT needs an evidence system separate from its scientific data.
Investors increasingly require evidence of impact as well as delivery.
MEAL now needs to prioritize compliance reports over scientific evidence.

questions.explanation: Investors ask what changed, how, for whom and why, alongside delivery outputs. The framework treats better evidence as a basis for funding, policy influence and sustained partnerships.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Read the opening explanation of why the MEAL approach is changing.

questions.question: A team wants to buy a survey platform before deciding what it needs to learn. What should it do first?

options.text: Define the question and the indicator’s evidence requirements.
Collect all available data and choose the question afterward.
Copy the most detailed questionnaire from another project.
Choose the platform with the largest number of form fields.

questions.explanation: The Capture function starts with the question and then identifies the required observations and context. The indicator method guides the choice of collection sources and tools.
questions.reviewTip: Use the Capture function to plan one question before selecting a tool.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the five evidence functions in the framework?

options.text: Planning, Capture, Reporting, Accountability, Evaluation
Capture, Quality Assurance, Integration, Analysis, Use and Visualization
Capture, Monitoring, Synthesis, Budgeting, Reporting
Capture, Quality Assurance, Evaluation, Accountability, Learning

questions.explanation: The five functions run across the results chain from collection to use. They organize evidence work and do not replace the four results levels.
questions.reviewTip: Review how the five evidence functions operate across all results levels.

questions.question: Leadership must decide where to allocate resources across regions. Which MEAL product best fits that decision?

options.text: A portfolio view of results, risks, reach and evidence gaps.
A complete list of outputs without outcomes or evidence gaps.
An unweighted ranking of project totals from different indicators.
Regional narratives without shared measurement definitions or comparable results.

questions.explanation: Portfolio leadership needs a coherent view across projects, regions and Thrusts. Section 6.1 connects that view to strategy and resource allocation.
questions.reviewTip: Match each institutional level to the decisions its evidence should support.

questions.question: A new study could use data from an earlier project. Which practice matches the intended 2030 capabilities?

options.text: Reuse the published total while discarding its measurement method.
Merge records based on their units without checking concepts or methods.
Repeat collection because each project must create its own evidence.
Reuse harmonized records with documented methods and quality.

questions.explanation: The framework aims to make data from one project useful for research and institutional analysis. Reuse depends on comparable definitions, traceable methods and documented quality.
questions.reviewTip: Review the links between comparability, traceability and data reuse.

questions.question: A project reports that it reached 5,000 farmers. What additional question best matches the framework’s intended 2030 shift?

options.text: What changed for those farmers, under which conditions, and what did CIMMYT contribute?
Did delivery match the annual workplan and approved spending?
How many project reports included the farmer-reach total?
How many activities did project staff complete during the reporting period?

questions.explanation: The framework asks CIMMYT to explain change, context, scale and contribution. A reach total describes delivery but does not answer those questions by itself.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the current and intended institutional questions in section 6.2.

questions.question: When should central MEAL first help develop a project’s theory of change?

options.text: During award and inception, after the proposal budget is fixed.
During the first quarterly review, once delivery has begun.
During system design, after indicators and collection tools are chosen.
During opportunity and proposal design.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle places theory-of-change work in opportunity and proposal design. MEAL enters before indicators, budgets and data systems become fixed.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the MEAL tasks and gate for opportunity and proposal design.

questions.question: Which package best matches the results architecture required at inception?

options.text: An activity schedule, annual budget and outputs without learning questions.
A theory of change or results chain, learning questions and strategy links.
An indicator list, targets and reporting dates without a results chain.
A collection plan, data flows and access rules without strategy links.

questions.explanation: The minimum package includes a theory of change or results chain, decision and learning questions, and links to CIMMYT Strategy. These elements guide the project’s evidence requirements.
questions.reviewTip: Review the results architecture element of the minimum package.

questions.question: A systems project assumes that new coordination meetings will change partner behavior. What should its theory-of-change review examine?

options.text: The meeting count as sufficient confirmation that partner behavior changed.
The assumed link between coordination and behavior, using stakeholder and context evidence.
The workplan completion rate as a substitute for checking partner behavior.
The project’s coordination budget as the full measure of systemic contribution.

questions.explanation: Annex A asks system-change projects to check their contribution and theory-of-change assumptions. This scenario applies that guidance to the link between coordination and behavior.
questions.reviewTip: Identify one assumption connecting a project activity to a systemic outcome.

questions.question: A digital advisory pilot tracks logins but aims to change farming practice. What should it add to its results logic?

options.text: An outcome target based only on total advice messages sent.
A plan to infer agronomic benefits from continued platform access.
A link from useful advice and engagement to adoption and behavior change.
A plan to equate repeat logins with repeated practice adoption.

questions.explanation: Annex A connects digital advisory usefulness and engagement with adoption and behavior change. Login counts can inform usage monitoring but cannot establish that full pathway alone.
questions.reviewTip: Review the digital agriculture and AI row of the MEAL Matrix.

questions.question: A variety performs well in trials. A team wants to claim that it has raised household incomes. What is missing from that reasoning?

options.text: A larger trial sample without adoption or household evidence.
An estimate that treats weather and market prices as irrelevant by definition.
Evidence linking the technology to lasting change alongside other factors.
A rule to extrapolate income gains directly from trial yield differences.

questions.explanation: The impact level requires evidence of CIMMYT’s contribution to lasting change alongside other factors. Applying that rule means trial performance alone does not establish household income impact.
questions.reviewTip: Trace the evidence needed between trial performance and household benefit.

questions.question: Which proposed pathway best applies the framework’s cumulative results logic to an agronomy project?

options.text: Deliver recommendations, count leaflet recipients, then classify reach as lasting impact.
Deliver recommendations, equate reach with adoption, then project household benefits.
Complete field visits, infer adoption from visit counts, then report income gains.
Deliver recommendations, examine changes in practice, then assess lasting benefits.

questions.explanation: The framework connects processes, outputs, outcomes and impact while giving each level a different evidential role. This pathway applies that logic without treating delivery as proof of lasting benefit.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Map one intervention across the four results levels.

questions.question: Evidence from a local systems project contradicts an assumption about partner cooperation. What fits the Matrix’s guidance?

options.text: Retain the pathway and consider the evidence only during endline reporting.
Treat additional meetings as sufficient confirmation of partner cooperation.
Review that assumption and the project’s contribution to systemic outcomes.
Revise output targets while leaving the partner-cooperation assumption untested.

questions.explanation: Annex A asks system-change projects to check assumptions and their contribution to systemic outcomes. Evidence that challenges an assumption provides a reason to review the proposed pathway.
questions.reviewTip: Check a theory-of-change assumption against current partner evidence.

questions.question: A discovery-science project struggles to describe its relevance beyond laboratory outputs. What does Annex A propose?

options.text: Delay MEAL until a later project begins field deployment.
Connect scientific advances to impact pathways and innovation readiness.
Use trial potential as a direct estimate of realized farmer adoption.
Replace pathway analysis with the number of laboratory outputs produced.

questions.explanation: The upstream discovery-science row links scientific advances to impact pathways and innovation readiness. It keeps monitoring appropriate to the research rather than assuming downstream benefits.
questions.reviewTip: Review how the Matrix connects upstream research to impact pathways.

questions.question: A seed pilot records seed distribution but has no way to examine whether its adoption logic holds. What support fits the Matrix?

options.text: Count every recipient as a confirmed long-term adopter.
Use distributed seed volume as the complete adoption estimate.
Define suitable KPIs and check the adoption and diffusion logic.
Treat seed availability as confirmation that farmers planted it.

questions.explanation: The seed-systems row calls for KPI definitions and a check of adoption and diffusion logic. Distribution records support delivery evidence but do not confirm adoption by themselves.
questions.reviewTip: Compare dissemination evidence with evidence that tests adoption logic.

questions.question: In the lifecycle RACI matrix, who is accountable for developing the theory of change and results framework?

options.text: The project lead
The Data Group
The Project MEAL Focal Point
The MEAL Review Committee

questions.explanation: The RACI matrix assigns accountability to the project lead and responsibility for the work to the Regional MEAL Lead. The relevant core pillars provide consultation.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Read the RACI row for the theory of change and results framework.

questions.question: Which sequence gives the four results levels in the framework?

options.text: Processes, Outputs, Outcomes, Impact
Inputs, Activities, Outputs, Impact
Processes, Outputs, Uptake, Reporting
Activities, Products, Learning, Impact

questions.explanation: The framework uses Processes, Outputs, Outcomes and Impact as its four results levels. The five evidence functions operate across those levels.

source.title: The MEAL Framework: From Data to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Distinguish the four results levels from the five evidence functions.

questions.question: A manager checks delayed procurement, workplan execution and financial tracking. Which results level is the focus?

options.text: Impact
Outputs
Outcomes
Processes

questions.explanation: Processes cover the management actions and day-to-day work that enable delivery. These records help teams address execution problems before they affect outcomes.
questions.reviewTip: Match workplan, finance and coordination records to process monitoring.

questions.question: A project has deployed a digital advisory tool and delivered training. Which results level describes these achievements?

options.text: Outputs
Impact
Processes
Outcomes

questions.explanation: The framework lists deployed digital tools and delivered training as outputs. Further evidence is needed to establish changes in use, practice or lasting benefit.
questions.reviewTip: Review the examples of products and services counted as outputs.

questions.question: Follow-up evidence shows that farmers changed their agronomic practices. Which results level does this most directly describe?

options.text: Outcomes
Outputs
Processes
Impact

questions.explanation: Outcomes include changes in behavior and agronomic practice among beneficiaries. Such a change does not by itself establish a positive, lasting impact.
questions.reviewTip: Compare a delivered recommendation with a change in farming practice.

questions.question: Which description matches impact in this framework?

options.text: Submission of the project’s quarterly reports.
Completion of the project’s scheduled activities.
Delivery of the project’s products and services.
Positive, lasting change in agrifood systems.

questions.explanation: Impact concerns lasting changes such as productivity, food security, resilience and inclusion. CIMMYT seeks credible evidence of its contribution alongside other causes.
questions.reviewTip: Review the impact definition and the limitation on sole-cause claims.

questions.question: A partner begins implementing a policy supported by the project. Which example in the framework best matches this result?

options.text: An impact through a lasting improvement in food security.
A process through coordination of policy meetings.
An outcome through policy implementation.
An output through delivery of policy advice.

questions.explanation: The framework explicitly lists policy implementation as an outcome. The result describes a change in a partner’s behavior or system.
questions.reviewTip: Review the policy and institutional examples at outcome level.

questions.question: An output dashboard lists 20 training events but gives no location, participants or delivery quality. What should the team improve?

options.text: Count each repeat attendance as new reach without checking participant identity.
Report the event total more frequently without adding delivery detail.
Relabel the event total as an estimate of farmer income impact.
Show where, to whom, how well and at what scale it delivered training.

questions.explanation: Output measurement should describe reach, coverage, quality and scale as well as delivery counts. This detail provides a basis for later outcome evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Check an output record for location, recipients, quality and scale.

questions.question: Two projects report participant reach under different investor formats. What inception document should show their links to institutional measures?

options.text: An output register storing delivery totals without mapping definitions.
An indicator crosswalk linking institutional, investor and project-specific measures.
A common report template giving different measures the same label.
A project workplan assigning reporting deadlines to focal points.

questions.explanation: The indicator crosswalk maps applicable institutional KPIs, investor indicators and project-specific measures. It should preserve institutional definitions rather than silently changing them.
questions.reviewTip: Review the indicator crosswalk element of the minimum package.

questions.question: Who primarily owns routine process and output evidence in the operating model?

options.text: The Data Group and system administrators.
The Regional MEAL Leads alone.
Project and program teams.
Central MEAL’s three technical pillars.

questions.explanation: Project and program teams own routine processes and outputs. Central MEAL supplies standards, quality support and integration for institutional use.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Review the ownership split for each results level.

questions.question: A project’s results framework lists indicators but omits how, when and from whom it will measure them. What should it complete?

options.text: A shared dashboard layout and common indicator naming convention.
A roll-up showing the volume and Thrust for each indicator.
A measurement plan with units, methods, coverage, timing and owners.
A longer indicator list and more frequent reporting deadlines.

questions.explanation: The minimum package requires a measurement plan for every indicator. The plan specifies sources, methods, frequency, coverage, disaggregation and responsibility.
questions.reviewTip: Check one indicator against the measurement-plan requirements.

questions.question: How does this version of the framework organize the KPI Toolbox?

options.text: 13 indicators in ten pathway volumes.
100 indicators in three reporting levels.
142 indicators in four evidence layers.
142 indicators in 13 pathway volumes.

questions.explanation: Section 3.1 states that the Toolbox contains 142 indicators in 13 volumes. Ten volumes cover impact pathways and three cover enabling pathways.
questions.reviewTip: Review the Toolbox structure in section 3.1.

questions.question: Which three Thrusts organize the impact-pathway volumes?

options.text: Monitoring, Evaluation and Accountability.
Productivity, Resource Mobilization and Reporting.
Human Wellbeing, Planetary Health and Peace.
Africa, Latin America and South Asia.

questions.explanation: The framework groups impact-pathway volumes under Human Wellbeing, Planetary Health and Peace. It reports enabling volumes alongside them as institutional performance.
questions.reviewTip: Locate the Thrust assigned to two different KPI volumes.

questions.question: Two projects measure the same concept in different contexts. What does KPI harmonization require?

options.text: Shared definitions, valid methods and rules for interpretation and aggregation.
A common indicator label even when the underlying concepts differ.
A single project total that replaces the underlying observations.
Identical field instruments in every context regardless of measurement level.

questions.explanation: Harmonization means projects share the concept, methodological logic and valid interpretation rules. The framework permits different suitable methods across measurement levels.

source.title: KPI Approach: Comparable and Fit for Purpose

questions.reviewTip: Review what harmonization requires and what it allows to vary.

questions.question: A trial team prepares yield records for comparison. Which practice matches the stated trial standards?

options.text: Average any available yields without recording protocols or plot sizes.
Use gross-plot harvests and omit moisture because all trials are controlled.
Use farmer recall as the trial standard without documenting the method.
Use net-plot yield, standard moisture and the required plot and repetition rules.

questions.explanation: The trial example requires net-plot measurement, moisture adjustment and plot-size or repetition standards. The stated moisture example is 12.5% for maize, not a universal value for every crop.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Read the trial and station row of the yield measurement example.

questions.question: An analyst combines farm and trial records into a regional yield estimate. Which plan best matches the framework?

options.text: Average source means without considering area or representativeness.
Pool all available records without defining eligibility or target population.
Add reported trial yields and divide by the number of projects.
Define inclusion rules, apply suitable weights and report uncertainty and coverage.

questions.explanation: Regional aggregation requires inclusion criteria, weighting by area or representativeness, and uncertainty bounds. Coverage and method quality affect how the estimate can be interpreted.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Review regional yield aggregation and its reporting requirements.

questions.question: A project wants to change an institutional indicator’s meaning to suit a local activity. What does the framework allow?

options.text: Specify local scope while preserving the institutional definition and approved method.
Change the definition quietly while keeping the institutional KPI label.
Choose whichever definition gives the largest reported achievement.
Use the local activity count as an equivalent measure without review.

questions.explanation: Projects may specify their local scope but must not silently redefine institutional indicators. Shared concepts and methods make evidence comparable across contexts.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Compare local scope choices with changes to an institutional definition.

questions.question: Which information belongs in a KPI’s measurement guidance?

options.text: Annual budget, staffing plan, activity calendar and report approval route only.
Collection platform, storage location, dashboard design and reporting audience only.
Indicator title, reporting target, final deadline and investor contact only.
Unit of observation, valid methods, aggregation rules, disaggregation and provenance.

questions.explanation: The framework specifies the concept, unit, sources, methods, calculation, aggregation, disaggregation, quality and provenance for each KPI. A label and target alone do not provide a measurement method.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Check a KPI reference sheet for method, calculation and provenance fields.

questions.question: Farm teams use crop cuts in one area and farmer surveys in another. What should accompany the yield records?

options.text: The method used and a documented quality rating.
A common yield unit with no distinction between measurement methods.
A single regional quality rating regardless of the source method.
The controlled-trial quality rating applied to both farm sources.

questions.explanation: The farm example allows feasible methods with different reliability. Teams should use the most reliable feasible method and record the method and quality rating.

source.title: One KPI, Multiple Valid Measurement Levels

questions.reviewTip: Review the farm and plot measurement standards for yield.

questions.question: Projects submit totals for the same institutional KPI. How should CIMMYT calculate the institutional result?

options.text: Select the highest project total to avoid double counting.
Sum every project total without examining overlap or eligibility.
Recompute from eligible records using the indicator’s approved aggregation method.
Average the totals while ignoring differences in units and populations.

questions.explanation: Institutional results come from eligible records under KPI-specific rules such as deduplication, weighting or modeling. The framework rules out an unqualified sum of project totals.

questions.reviewTip: Identify the aggregation rule before combining project evidence.

questions.question: How should Volume 1, Innovation development and scaling, relate to the three Thrusts?

options.text: It applies only to Human Wellbeing.
It applies across all three Thrusts.
It replaces all three Thrusts in reporting.
It belongs to the enabling volumes.

questions.explanation: Volume 1 is cross-cutting because innovations and partnerships feed every pathway. The other volume assignments do not remove this cross-Thrust role.
questions.reviewTip: Review Volume 1 and the explanation below the volume table.

questions.question: Which set lists the quality dimensions in the Five Evidence Functions?

options.text: Precision, profitability, reach, adoption, resilience and inclusion.
Validity, efficiency, cost, relevance, coherence and sustainability.
Coverage, speed, staff capacity, reporting volume, cost and engagement.
Completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and representativeness.

questions.explanation: Quality Assurance covers these six dimensions along with validation, standardization and provenance. A large dataset can still fail one or more quality checks.
questions.reviewTip: Apply the six quality dimensions to one collection process.

questions.question: The same farmer joins two projects in consecutive years. What system feature best supports checking for double counting?

options.text: A new farmer number in every project report.
A larger annual total that includes both entries.
A participant name field with no matching rules.
A stable farmer identifier used across projects and years.

questions.explanation: Persistent identifiers link the same entity across projects and years. They support deduplication and links between delivery, later uptake and outcomes.
questions.reviewTip: Review the persistent-identifier requirement and its purpose.

questions.question: An outcome dataset has missing values and unusual observations. What should the team do before comparing projects?

options.text: Delete every unusual observation without checking its cause.
Treat each missing value as a confirmed zero outcome.
Publish comparisons without recording the data limitations.
Investigate quality issues and check consistency and comparability.

questions.explanation: Outcome-level quality work addresses missing values, outliers, consistency and comparability. Investigation protects interpretation without assuming that every unusual value is wrong.
questions.reviewTip: Review the outcome-level quality tasks before comparing datasets.

questions.question: A survey covers only easily reached farms, but the team wants to generalize to the whole region. Which quality concern needs attention?

options.text: Consistency of the recorded measurement units.
Timeliness of the collected observations.
Representativeness of the observed farms.
Uniqueness of the farmer identifiers.

questions.explanation: Representativeness is one of the required quality controls. This scenario applies that control to whether the observed farms support the intended regional claim.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the observed population with the population named in the claim.

questions.question: An auditor asks how an institutional result was produced. Which records best support the answer?

options.text: Source-level provenance, quality flags and a record of changes.
A total copied into several reports with no calculation trail.
The final dashboard image without its source records.
A statement that an experienced analyst checked the result.

questions.explanation: The system requires provenance and an audit trail at record level. These features allow institutional figures to be audited and recalculated.
questions.reviewTip: Trace a reported figure back to source records and documented changes.

questions.question: A field form accepts impossible values with no warning. Which required functionality should address this close to collection?

options.text: Entry validation with range and consistency checks.
A new reporting template using the same unchecked fields.
An endline comparison of average values across locations.
A dashboard refresh that updates before checks occur.

questions.explanation: The system requires validation at entry and automated range and consistency checks. Detecting errors near collection supports timely correction and a documented quality trail.
questions.reviewTip: Review the automated checks required under quality assurance and provenance.

questions.question: A team improves its KPI calculation method and wants to rerun last year’s result. What makes this possible?

options.text: Keeping old-method summaries without record-level provenance.
Retaining the underlying records and their provenance.
Keeping dashboard exports without the underlying observations.
Keeping project totals as substitutes for the source observations.

questions.explanation: The framework retains underlying records and provenance so results can be recalculated as methods improve. A rounded total alone cannot support that re-analysis.
questions.reviewTip: Review why the framework keeps records beneath reported summaries.

questions.question: What is the normal purpose of continuous or monthly assurance in the operating cadence?

options.text: Check data quality and resolve exceptions close to collection.
Recompute every institutional KPI with a new method each month.
Conduct a full counterfactual study for each project every month.
Review source data only when investors query an annual total.

questions.explanation: Continuous or monthly work covers routine checks and timely resolution of exceptions. Typical outputs include quality flags, corrected records and a system issue log.
questions.reviewTip: Review the continuous and monthly row of the cadence table.

questions.question: Who runs first-line quality checks and maintains source evidence close to project implementation?

options.text: The Data Group without the project team’s involvement.
The Project MEAL Focal Point with the project team.
The Evaluation and Research Specialist for all project records.
The Core Layer’s evidence systems pillar alone.

questions.explanation: Project MEAL Focal Points coordinate monitoring, keep source records and run first-line quality checks. They receive technical guidance from the Regional MEAL Lead.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Project MEAL Focal Point responsibilities.

questions.question: Several regions report recurring deduplication problems. Which core role maintains the relevant rules and supports remediation?

options.text: Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst.
Evaluation and Research Specialist.
MEAL Enablement and Backstopping Officer.
Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst.

questions.explanation: The Evidence Systems, Data Quality and Reporting Analyst maintains validation, deduplication and provenance rules. The role also monitors recurrent quality issues and works with regions to resolve gaps.
questions.reviewTip: Locate the analyst responsible for data-quality rules and remediation.

questions.question: In the Evidence Stack, which layer includes plot, household, trial and participant records?

options.text: External and context data
Operational records
Direct observations
Earth observation and sensors

questions.explanation: Direct observations provide evidence close to the state or change being measured. Their detail supports disaggregation and re-analysis.
questions.reviewTip: Review the four evidence layers and their example sources.

questions.question: A team wants to map land under a practice using satellite imagery. What example use does the framework describe?

options.text: Treat any vegetation signal as proof that the practice was adopted.
Discard field observations because imagery covers a larger area.
Use imagery from any year as a substitute for the reporting period.
Calibrate the mapping with ground observations under documented rules.

questions.explanation: The Evidence Stack describes mapping land under practices after calibration with ground observations. Satellite data must respect the KPI method and compatible definitions.
questions.reviewTip: Review the earth-observation example and triangulation rule.

questions.question: An analyst adds rainfall, prices and national statistics to interpret productivity change. Which evidence layer provides this context?

options.text: Direct participant observations
External and context data
Operational training records
Internal workplan tracking

questions.explanation: External and context data supply benchmarks, denominators and variables that help interpret change. They complement the measurement rather than proving project contribution alone.
questions.reviewTip: Match rainfall, market and national data to their analytical purpose.

questions.question: Researchers want to link who received a service with later uptake. Which evidence layer records the delivery side of that link?

options.text: Operational records such as training and distribution logs.
National statistics without intervention histories.
External price series without participant identifiers.
Satellite imagery without records of service recipients.

questions.explanation: Operational records connect interventions and outputs to later outcomes. Linking them to uptake evidence requires compatible records and suitable identifiers.
questions.reviewTip: Review how operational records link delivery with later change.

questions.question: Breeding data already sit in an authoritative scientific system. How should the MEAL data system use them?

options.text: Connect to the authoritative system through appropriate integration.
Require staff to copy every record into unrelated project spreadsheets.
Replace the scientific system solely to create a MEAL dashboard.
Ignore the data because MEAL only accepts new field surveys.

questions.explanation: The framework connects MEAL to authoritative scientific and corporate systems. It does not require replacing those systems or copying their data by hand.
questions.reviewTip: Identify the authoritative system before designing a new data flow.

questions.question: Field teams often work without a reliable connection. Which design principle should shape their collection system?

options.text: Transfer collection to partners whenever internet service fails.
Support offline work through shared, configurable components.
Use an online-only form and delay capture until teams return.
Configure projects independently without shared components or definitions.

questions.explanation: The framework requires offline operation where connectivity is poor and modular shared components. Collection methods still need to meet the KPI requirements.
questions.reviewTip: Review offline operation, modularity and open standards in section 4.2.

questions.question: An investor introduces a new reporting template for data CIMMYT already collects. What should change first?

options.text: The institutional KPI definition to match the template’s layout.
Every field form, even when the required source variables already exist.
The central mapping from source variables to required reporting fields.
The project’s source records so they resemble the final report.

questions.explanation: The MEAL team maps reporting requirements to validated source variables. It adapts mappings or exports so projects avoid collecting or entering the same evidence again.

source.title: Alignment with Investor Reporting Systems: Collect Data Once

questions.reviewTip: Review how the collect-once approach handles a new reporting system.

questions.question: What should the KPI engine report alongside an institutional result?

options.text: Only project targets and the number of submitting teams.
Only the largest project total and its publication date.
Only a point estimate and its reporting deadline.
Coverage, uncertainty and the method version used.

questions.explanation: The KPI engine uses eligible records and the approved method. It reports coverage, uncertainty and method version so users can interpret the result.
questions.reviewTip: Read the KPI engine functionality and its reporting requirements.

questions.question: A manager wants to see whether a recommendation led to action. Which system feature should support this?

options.text: Training attendance on the topic without management-response records.
The number of reports that repeat the recommendation.
Decision logs and management responses linked to the underlying evidence.
Dashboard refresh dates without records of subsequent decisions.

questions.explanation: The learning and feedback functionality links decisions, management responses and participant feedback to evidence. This connection helps close the loop from analysis to action.
questions.reviewTip: Review the learning and feedback functionality in the data system.

questions.question: How does the framework divide ownership of the MEAL data system?

options.text: The Data Group owns infrastructure; MEAL owns indicators, the dictionary and quality rules.
Investors own the source records; the review committee writes collection software.
MEAL owns all software engineering; projects own institutional KPI definitions.
Each project owns separate institutional standards; the Data Group approves impact claims.

questions.explanation: Section 4.2 assigns infrastructure to the Data Group and content to MEAL. Section 5.9 keeps specialist technical capabilities in the relevant technical functions.
questions.reviewTip: Review the ownership split before assigning system-development responsibilities.

questions.question: What kind of impact claim does CIMMYT seek under the framework?

options.text: A claim that CIMMYT alone caused every observed positive change.
A claim based entirely on whether the project met its spending plan.
A credible account of its contribution alongside other factors.
A delivery total used as proof of lasting household benefit.

questions.explanation: The framework seeks evidence of the role CIMMYT’s technologies, partnerships, capacity and services played. It explicitly rejects treating CIMMYT as the sole cause of observed changes.
questions.reviewTip: Review how the framework describes credible contribution to impact.

questions.question: An evaluation observes rising yields during a period of unusually favorable rainfall and prices. How should it approach the impact claim?

options.text: Assign the full yield increase to CIMMYT because farmers joined the project.
Ignore climate and market data because they come from external sources.
Use the number of field visits as the estimate of yield impact.
Analyze intervention evidence together with relevant climate and market context.

questions.explanation: Impact integration links interventions and outcomes with contextual, climate and market information. This scenario applies the requirement to interpret contribution alongside other factors.
questions.reviewTip: List the contextual factors that could affect the result being assessed.

questions.question: A team asks what CIMMYT contributed to yield change in Kenya. Which approach matches the framework’s example?

options.text: Add project yield-change totals and treat the sum as national contribution.
Compare yield averages without a credible reference or adoption evidence.
Use suitable contribution or attribution analysis with adoption, context and a credible counterfactual.
Count released varieties and assume equal national yield effects for each.

questions.explanation: The example calls for contribution or attribution analysis against a credible counterfactual with modeling, adoption and geospatial evidence. A sum of reported numbers cannot answer that causal question.

source.title: From Observation-Level Data to Decision-Relevant Insights

questions.reviewTip: Review the Kenya yield-change example and its evidence requirements.

questions.question: Two datasets show similar trends but cover different populations and years. Can the team treat their agreement as triangulation?

options.text: Only after replacing both datasets with their project report totals.
Yes, if the larger dataset contains more observations than the smaller one.
Only after checking construct, population, geography, period and definition compatibility.
Yes, because similar trend directions establish the same impact in any population.

questions.explanation: A source strengthens a claim when it measures compatible constructs, populations, places and periods. Similar-looking trends alone do not meet the triangulation rule.
questions.reviewTip: Apply every part of the triangulation rule before combining sources.

questions.question: A KPI method requires direct ground measurement, but satellite data are cheaper. What should the team do?

options.text: Replace the measurement without review because imagery is available more often.
Keep the required ground measurement and use imagery in valid supporting roles.
Report modeled values as direct observations without documenting the change.
Treat satellite coverage as proof that ground calibration is unnecessary.

questions.explanation: Satellite and secondary data do not replace ground observations when the method requires direct measurement. The framework allows supporting uses such as calibration, context and documented upscaling.
questions.reviewTip: Review the limit on substituting satellite data for required ground observations.

questions.question: Which methods does the framework include for impact analysis?

options.text: Descriptive totals alone, without evaluating contribution or context.
Participant-reach estimates alone, without examining lasting change.
Counterfactual evaluation, contribution analysis, geospatial assessment and modeling.
Delivery counts and budget execution as direct substitutes for outcome evidence.

questions.explanation: Impact analysis can use counterfactual, attribution, contribution, geospatial, modeling and scenario methods. Teams must choose methods that match the question and the intended claim.
questions.reviewTip: Review the impact methods and consider what each can help answer.

questions.question: A project plans an outcome study that requires a baseline or valid reference. When should it address that need?

options.text: At closure, by treating the target as the observed baseline.
During design and inception, with a documented alternative if the method permits.
Only after final results show whether the project appears successful.
After reporting impact, by assuming the starting value was zero.

questions.explanation: The minimum package requires a baseline, comparison group or other valid reference when the method calls for one. It also allows a documented alternative rather than leaving the issue to final reporting.
questions.reviewTip: Review the baseline and reference requirement in the minimum package.

questions.question: An impact analysis has limited coverage and substantial uncertainty. What should accompany the findings?

options.text: A precise-looking result with the uncertainty removed from the report.
A point estimate with coverage limits reserved for internal files.
A claim of universal effects based on the available subset.
An explicit account of uncertainty and the limits of the claim.

questions.explanation: The Analysis function requires methods that match the question and claim. It also requires explicit documentation of uncertainty and limits.
questions.reviewTip: Check that an analytical claim states its uncertainty and limits.

questions.question: How does section 5.2 allocate primary responsibility for impact evidence?

options.text: Central MEAL with science/evaluation specialists; projects provide records and context.
Project leads alone, using only routine output monitoring.
Regional project teams alone, without science or evaluation input.
The Data Group alone, using system completeness checks.

questions.explanation: Central MEAL works with science and evaluation specialists on impact methods and synthesis. Projects contribute source data, context and implementation history.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Review the impact row in the division-of-responsibility table.

questions.question: A severe shock changes conditions midway through a project. Which cadence provision could support a relevant impact study?

options.text: A monthly activity total used instead of outcome measurement.
Trigger-based measurement when relevant to the event.
A rule that evaluations can occur only at project closure.
A requirement to exclude shocks from contribution analysis.

questions.explanation: The cadence includes trigger-based outcome or impact studies and relevant shock-event measurement. The study still needs a suitable question, design and evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Review the midterm, endline and trigger-based row of the cadence table.

questions.question: What should a quarterly or seasonal evidence review normally produce?

options.text: An annual reporting schedule without decisions on current evidence.
An updated indicator list without recording implementation decisions.
A review pack summarizing findings without assigning follow-up actions.
A decision log stating changes, action owners and deadlines.

questions.explanation: Quarterly or seasonal reviews focus on implementation, reach, uptake and emerging outcomes. The stated output records what changes, who acts and by when.
questions.reviewTip: Review the quarterly and seasonal cadence and its decision-log output.

questions.question: A dashboard shows low early uptake halfway through implementation. What best reflects adaptive management?

options.text: Wait for annual reporting before considering an implementation change.
Review the evidence, adjust delivery and document actions for follow-up.
Increase reporting frequency without reviewing reasons for low uptake.
Treat completed delivery targets as sufficient grounds to continue unchanged.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle asks teams to use evidence reviews to adapt implementation and document decisions. The required review gate includes actions, owners and follow-up.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Review the implementation and adaptive-management phase and its gate.

questions.question: An evaluation report recommends a change, but no one records a response. Which responsibility addresses this gap?

options.text: Count report delivery as the completed management response.
Record the recommendation without checking whether anyone acts on it.
Assign the findings to the next evaluation without naming an action owner.
Translate findings into management responses and track significant recommendations.

questions.explanation: Pillar C must turn evaluation findings into management responses. It also tracks whether teams act on significant recommendations.
questions.reviewTip: Review the Evaluation, Learning and Accountability pillar’s follow-up duties.

questions.question: Two projects show different results in similar interventions. What should a learning review examine?

options.text: Rank projects by their reported totals without examining context.
Pool the results immediately so regional differences no longer appear.
Repeat the same intervention without reviewing the difference.
Why results differ across contexts and what the evidence supports changing.

questions.explanation: Pillar C examines whether outcomes occur and why results differ across contexts. Its purpose includes turning evidence into learning and action.
questions.reviewTip: Review the evaluative questions assigned to Pillar C.

questions.question: Which annual products help CIMMYT see both institutional results and missing evidence?

options.text: An investor submission, training calendar and project contact list.
A portfolio total without coverage, uncertainty or method information.
A portfolio dashboard, evidence-gap register and method notes.
A project output ledger, annual target list and reporting calendar.

questions.explanation: The annual cadence recomputes KPIs from eligible records and reviews coverage, uncertainty and gaps. It produces a portfolio dashboard, evidence-gap register and method notes.
questions.reviewTip: Review the annual cadence and the purpose of the evidence-gap register.

questions.question: Field staff repeatedly ask how to apply one indicator. Which support approach fits the framework?

options.text: Use practical guidance, refresher sessions and office hours, and log recurring issues.
Let each project write its own guidance without common review.
Issue one indicator handout and wait for the annual report review.
Refer every routine question directly to an external evaluation consultant.

questions.explanation: The Enablement and Backstopping Officer maintains practical resources, clinics, office hours and support logs. Recurrent issues can then be escalated for technical attention.
questions.reviewTip: Review the enablement role’s training and first-line support functions.

questions.question: A pilot reveals that a collection procedure is impractical in the field. What should the rollout do with that finding?

options.text: Refine the guidance and tools using evidence from the pilot.
Expand implementation and review field feasibility at project closure.
Replace the institutional definition locally without recording a method change.
Keep the procedure unchanged until every region completes rollout.

questions.explanation: The rollout uses real project pilots to test KPIs, methods and collection. It explicitly calls for refining tools and guidance based on what pilots show.
questions.reviewTip: Review the pilot milestone and how pilot evidence informs refinement.

questions.question: A team holds regular learning meetings, but evidence never changes practice or guidance. Which enabling condition is weak?

options.text: Capacity development.
Strong data systems.
Continuous learning and adaptation.
Clear roles and governance.

questions.explanation: The enabling conditions call for teams to review and act on evidence. They also call for improvements to appear in new versions of the guidance.
questions.reviewTip: Check whether evidence reviews lead to actions and updated guidance.

questions.question: What does the handover phase require beyond delivering training?

options.text: Publication of a dashboard before testing the data system.
An attendance list alone, with ownership decided at closure.
Transfer of all routine project monitoring to the Core Layer.
A competency check, a live system and named data or MEAL owners.

questions.explanation: The handover gate includes competency, a functioning system and named owners. Training alone does not establish readiness for routine implementation.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Review the Enable and hand over phase and its required gate.

questions.question: Scientists want to learn across sites without rebuilding datasets for every study. Which intended value supports this?

options.text: Access to harmonized datasets and documented methods for synthesis and comparison.
Separate incompatible definitions tailored to every publication.
Access only to each project’s rounded annual reporting totals.
Removal of source methods once findings receive management approval.

questions.explanation: The Science and Impact value statement supports synthesis, modeling, evaluation and cross-site comparison. Harmonized data and documented methods help make that work possible.
questions.reviewTip: Review how the framework supports science and cross-site learning.

questions.question: Which set matches the four directions of accountability in the framework?

options.text: Investors and partners; national regulators; service providers; project staff.
Investors and partners; farmers and communities; science and CGIAR; internal teams and leadership.
Investors and partners; project staff; regional managers; senior leadership.
Scientific collaborators; CGIAR centers; journal reviewers; research funders.

questions.explanation: Accountability runs to investors and partners, farmers and communities, the scientific community and CGIAR, and internal actors. Each group needs evidence and responses suited to its role.
questions.reviewTip: Review all four rows of the accountability table.

questions.question: A project meets reporting deadlines but never returns findings to participating communities. What is missing?

options.text: More frequent reporting to project leadership alone.
Feedback that returns relevant evidence to the people it concerns.
Another investor template containing the same delivery totals.
A larger list of publications without community communication.

questions.explanation: Accountability to farmers and communities includes feedback mechanisms that return evidence to them. Timely investor reporting does not cover that separate responsibility.
questions.reviewTip: Review the farmer and community accountability requirements.

questions.question: Average outcomes improved, but the team has not examined who benefited. Which analysis best addresses inclusion?

options.text: Assess inclusion from activity totals without examining subgroup outcomes.
Disaggregate evidence by gender, age and relevant vulnerability dimensions.
Report only the pooled average because subgroup results may differ.
Use participant counts as the main evidence of benefit across groups.

questions.explanation: The framework requires attention to gender, age and other equity dimensions. Disaggregation helps reveal who benefits and who may be excluded.
questions.reviewTip: Review the equity dimensions relevant to your participant population.

questions.question: A study finds no benefit for a group the project intended to serve. What does accountability require?

options.text: Replace the measured outcome with the number of people contacted.
Omit the group because the overall project account should stay positive.
Report the finding openly and explain what the evidence shows.
Delay disclosure until the group’s result matches the target.

questions.explanation: The framework calls for openness about real benefits and about situations where benefits do not occur. This honesty applies to communities as well as investors and internal audiences.
questions.reviewTip: Review the requirement to explain what works and what does not.

questions.question: Which practices support accountability to the scientific community and CGIAR?

options.text: Documented methods, reproducible evidence and FAIR data practices.
Reporting delivery totals without data or method publication.
Circulating results internally without reproducible analysis documentation.
Publishing summary findings without specifying source methods.

questions.explanation: Scientific accountability requires rigor, reproducibility and transparency. The framework supports documented methods and publication of datasets and findings within the applicable data rules.
questions.reviewTip: Review the scientific accountability row and its supporting practices.

questions.question: A partner requests participant records for a joint analysis. Which system requirements should govern access?

options.text: Open access to all personal records because the partner works with CIMMYT.
A verbal request without checking consent or access permissions.
Consent records, role-based access and agreed data-sharing rules.
Automatic transfer of all records before defining the analysis purpose.

questions.explanation: The required functionality includes consent, role-based access, personal-data protection and partner data-sharing rules. A shared research purpose does not remove these requirements.
questions.reviewTip: Review the privacy, consent and access requirements before sharing records.

questions.question: How does the framework describe internal accountability?

options.text: Regional leads answer for each routine record; projects answer only for reporting dates.
Teams answer for their processes and outputs; leadership answers for portfolio-level results.
Projects answer for portfolio results; leadership answers only for activity delivery.
The Core Layer answers for all delivery; projects supply reports without source evidence.

questions.explanation: Individuals, leads and teams are accountable for work within their remit. Leadership holds accountability for portfolio-level results.
questions.reviewTip: Review the internal accountability row and its division of responsibility.

questions.question: Participants submit feedback about poor service access. How should the system help make that feedback actionable?

options.text: Report a feedback count without linking it to the issues raised.
Link the feedback to evidence, management responses and follow-up decisions.
Store participant feedback in a separate file without response records.
Summarize feedback at closure without recording management decisions.

questions.explanation: The learning and feedback functionality connects participant feedback with decisions and management responses. This makes the response traceable to the evidence that prompted it.
questions.reviewTip: Review how feedback connects to decision and management-response records.

questions.question: A project is preparing to collect personal data. What must its system-and-protocol gate cover?

options.text: A finished dashboard while consent arrangements remain undecided.
Tested collection, approved protocols, roles, consent and quality procedures.
Approval of target numbers without assigning collection responsibilities.
A reporting template without testing the collection workflow.

questions.explanation: The design gate requires a tested data system and approved protocols, roles, consent and QA procedures. These requirements belong before routine collection starts.

source.title: Project Lifecycle: MEAL from Proposal to Impact

questions.reviewTip: Review the system and protocol design gate before field collection.

questions.question: An investor asks for evidence that can be compared across projects. Which accountability support does the framework propose?

options.text: A single total with no information on methods or coverage.
Project-specific definitions with matching indicator labels.
Harmonized KPIs, documented methods and governed data quality.
Success stories selected without examining underlying evidence.

questions.explanation: Investor accountability requires transparent, timely and comparable reporting. Harmonized KPIs and documented quality support credible institutional evidence.
questions.reviewTip: Review the methods and quality requirements for investor accountability.

questions.question: What determines a project’s default M&E complexity in the MEAL Matrix?

options.text: Project type and its applicable mix of output, outcome and impact KPIs.
Investor report frequency alone, regardless of the project’s evidence needs.
The number of participating countries alone, regardless of applicable KPIs.
Project budget alone, without considering the required results levels.

questions.explanation: The Matrix uses project type and the number and levels of applicable KPIs to set default complexity. The Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification during proposal review.
questions.reviewTip: Review how the Matrix combines project type, complexity and scale.

questions.question: An Intermediate-complexity digital project commits to its own ground measurement of outcomes. What does the Matrix adjustment rule require?

options.text: Move up one complexity level to Complex.
Move down one level because the data come directly from the field.
Become MEGA regardless of the project’s budget and scale.
Remain Intermediate because the project type cannot change.

questions.explanation: The adjustment rule moves a project up one complexity level when it conducts its own ground outcome measurement. This rule adjusts complexity, not the project’s scale classification.
questions.reviewTip: Review all three triggers in the Matrix adjustment rule.

questions.question: A Small breeding project remains at its default Intermediate complexity. What base MEAL amount does section 5.10 specify?

options.text: USD 8,000 per project.
USD 13,000 per project.
USD 18,000 per project.
USD 27,000 per project year.

questions.explanation: The Small-project base amounts are USD 8,000, 13,000 and 18,000 for Standard, Intermediate and Complex work. The breeding row in Annex A uses Intermediate as the default classification.
questions.reviewTip: Review the Small-project budget row and the breeding classification in Annex A.

questions.question: A Medium project has a USD 300,000 budget and confirmed Complex M&E needs. What base contribution follows the percentage and minimum rules?

options.text: USD 15,000, because 5% applies without any minimum amount.
USD 13,000, because all Medium projects use the Intermediate minimum.
USD 9,000, because every Medium project contributes 3% of its budget.
USD 18,000, because the Small Complex minimum exceeds 5% of the budget.

questions.explanation: Five percent of USD 300,000 is USD 15,000, below the USD 18,000 Complex minimum. The project therefore budgets at least USD 18,000 and confirms the budget with MEAL during proposal writing.
questions.reviewTip: Apply both the percentage and same-complexity minimum for Medium projects.

questions.question: According to section 5.10, how should a MEGA project budget for MEAL?

options.text: Apply the Medium Standard percentage without discussing project needs.
Budget only for the final report after the project receives funding.
Apply a fixed USD 8,000 total with no project-specific MEAL costs.
Co-design the work and include at least USD 27,000 per year of institutional staff time.

questions.explanation: MEGA budgets are co-designed from proposal development and cover project-specific MEAL work. Section 5.10 also sets an institutional contribution of at least USD 27,000 per project year as Core Layer staff time.
questions.reviewTip: Review the MEGA row and distinguish institutional from project-specific costs.

questions.question: A project develops a useful local indicator and wants to report it as an institutional KPI. What must happen first?

options.text: The Data Group may rename it without a methodological review.
The Design, Standards and Enablement pillar must review and approve it.
The project may add it directly once its own lead approves the report.
The investor’s use of the label automatically makes it institutional.

questions.explanation: Projects can add local indicators, but institutional use requires the stated MEAL review and approval. Approved changes appear in a new Handbook version.
questions.reviewTip: Review the first governance rule for adding or redefining institutional KPIs.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly assigns methodological exceptions and annual institutional endorsement?

options.text: MEAL Group Lead: KPI method exceptions; MEAL Review Committee: annual endorsement.
Project lead: KPI method exceptions; Extended MEAL Network: annual endorsement.
Regional MEAL Lead: KPI method exceptions; MEAL Group Lead: annual endorsement.
Design, Standards and Enablement pillar: all exceptions; Data Group: annual endorsement.

questions.explanation: The MEAL Group Lead is accountable for method exceptions and implementation of Handbook changes. The institutional MEAL Review Committee reviews and endorses the annual changes.
questions.reviewTip: Review the governance rule on decisions, exceptions and annual review.

questions.question: Which assignment matches the three core pillars?

options.text: A: design and standards; B: evaluation and learning; C: evidence systems and performance.
A: evidence systems and performance; B: evaluation and learning; C: design and standards.
A: design and standards; B: evidence systems and performance; C: evaluation, learning and accountability.
A: evaluation and learning; B: design and standards; C: evidence systems and performance.

questions.explanation: Pillar A sets design and measurement standards, Pillar B manages evidence requirements and portfolio performance, and Pillar C leads evaluation and learning. Projects keep responsibility for routine monitoring.
questions.reviewTip: Review the purpose and handoffs of the three core pillars.

questions.question: What does the published roadmap require for all new proposals from October 2026?

options.text: Apply MEAL only if the proposal exceeds USD 10 million.
Use the KPI Toolbox and MEAL guidance during proposal design.
Delay MEAL design until the final investor report is due.
Use only project-specific indicators without an institutional crosswalk.

questions.explanation: The roadmap states that all new proposals use the Toolbox and guidance from October 2026. Teams should include collection, assurance, analysis and learning costs from the outset.
questions.reviewTip: Review the Apply in project proposals milestone and entry point.

questions.question: An ongoing project has more than two years left and wants to pilot the KPI system. What else does selection require?

options.text: A readiness diagnostic and checks on budget flexibility, system maturity and team capacity.
Acceptance based only on the number of countries listed in its proposal.
Immediate replacement of all current indicators before reviewing the project.
Selection by remaining duration alone, without checking existing data systems.

questions.explanation: The pilot entry point adds a readiness diagnostic and selection checks beyond remaining duration. Confirmed pilots then map existing indicators to the Toolbox in a crosswalk workshop.
questions.reviewTip: Review the pilot selection checks and the confirmed-pilot crosswalk step.

questions.question: On its own, what can a project report confirm, according to section 1?

options.text: That training took place or farmers were reached, not whether practices or yields changed
That yields improved for participants, but not which farmers were trained
That practices changed, provided the figures were aggregated across projects
That benefits persisted, as long as the report was submitted on time

questions.explanation: A report can confirm that training took place or that farmers were reached. It cannot by itself show whether practices changed, yields improved, risks declined or benefits persisted, which is why the new approach works from observation-level records.

questions.reviewTip: Reread the third paragraph of section 1 and underline what a report cannot show.

questions.question: A regional team spends most of each quarter compiling activity figures for investor templates and has no time to look at what the data say. Which change in section 1.1 addresses this directly?

options.text: From siloed information to integrated data systems
From time-consuming compliance reporting to high-frequency insights for decisions and learning
From work that is hard to link to strategy to credible evidence of contribution
From limited analysis to stronger aggregation and evidence

questions.explanation: The fourth row of the FROM/TO table moves from time-consuming reporting for compliance to high-frequency insights for better decision-making and learning. questions.question: Which strategic effect does the framework describe as integrated systems connecting science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management?

options.text: Evidence
Agility and foresight
Impact
Collaboration

questions.explanation: Collaboration is the effect about integrated systems that connect science, MEAL, data, KMIT and management. Evidence is about quality data, agility and foresight about timely insights, and impact about credible evidence of contribution.
questions.reviewTip: Learn the one-line description of each of the four strategic effects in section 1.2.

questions.question: A wheat team in South Asia sees from mid-season sowing-date records that advice is not reaching one district, and changes its extension plan before sowing ends. Which strategic effect is at work?

options.text: Evidence
Impact
Agility and foresight
Collaboration

questions.question: Why does the framework say MEAL at CIMMYT is different from MEAL in a typical service-delivery organisation?

options.text: CIMMYT reports to more investors than a delivery organisation does
CIMMYT's projects are too small for outcome measurement
CIMMYT's evidence is mostly about training delivered to farmers
Most of CIMMYT's evidence concerns scientific contribution to change in agrifood systems

questions.explanation: Section 1.3 says most of the evidence CIMMYT produces concerns scientific contribution to change in agrifood systems, more than service delivery. Its trial, adoption, genomic, remote-sensing, agronomic and socioeconomic data are the asset MEAL has to connect.

questions.reviewTip: Read the second paragraph of 1.3 and list the six kinds of data it names.

questions.question: A maize breeding team in Kenya holds multi-environment trial results. A socioeconomics team holds an adoption survey. A seed company holds sales records. What does section 1.3 say connecting these makes possible?

options.text: Credible claims of CIMMYT's contribution to yield gains, and learning that improves breeding decisions
A larger farmer-reach total, because sales records can replace the adoption survey
Three separate reports, one per team, submitted to the same investor
Proof that the breeding team alone caused the yield change in every district

Sales records add to the picture but do not replace the survey, and nothing in the framework claims sole causation.

source.title: MEAL in the Context of CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Study the three columns of the table in 1.3: assets, what gets connected, what becomes possible.

questions.question: Which evidence function recomputes institutional indicators from the underlying eligible records rather than summing project reports?

options.text: Capture
Quality assurance
Integration
Analysis

questions.reviewTip: Read the Integration row of the table in 2.5 and note its last sentence.

questions.question: A field officer in Mexico removes duplicate entries from a seed-recipient registry and records where each entry came from. Which evidence function is this?

options.text: Capture
Quality assurance
Analysis
Use and visualization

questions.question: Section 2.7 says accountability runs in four directions. Which list names them?

options.text: Investors and institutional partners; farmers, communities and stakeholders; the scientific community and CGIAR; internal
Investors and foundations; national governments; the media; the MEAL Review Committee
Investors and auditors; the Data Group; project leads; external evaluators
Farmers and households; seed companies; extension services; regional leadership

questions.explanation: The four directions are investors and institutional partners, farmers and communities, the scientific community and CGIAR, and internal accountability within CIMMYT. Each has different requirements and different ways MEAL supports it.

questions.question: How does the framework want MEAL to be perceived by 2030?

options.text: As a compliance function run by the central team
As an investor-reporting service charged at cost
As a data product owned by the Data Group
As a strategic institutional capability

questions.explanation: The 2030 box in section 6 says MEAL will no longer be perceived as a compliance function but as a strategic institutional capability. Reporting and data systems are part of it, but they are not what it is for.
questions.reviewTip: Read the 'Where will CIMMYT be by 2030?' box at the start of section 6.

questions.question: Two maize projects in Kenya each report a 20% yield gain. Project A cites its annual report. Project B can show plot records from crop cuts, farmer identifiers, dates and locations. Under the new approach, what is the difference?

options.text: None: a report and plot records are equal units of evidence
B's claim is traceable to observation-level records that can be analysed and reused
A is stronger because an aggregated figure is easier to compare
Neither counts until an investor has audited the figures

questions.explanation: The new approach builds a traceable body of evidence from observation-level records, so B's figure can be reconstructed, disaggregated and reused. A's report can confirm that something was delivered, but not what changed on the ground.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Ask of any headline figure: which records could I trace it back to?

questions.question: A project lead concludes that the new approach means quarterly reports will be abolished. What does section 1 actually say?

options.text: Reports are replaced by dashboards and no longer written
Reports stay as the primary unit of evidence for institutional figures
Reports stay, but only for investors who contractually require them
Reporting summaries stay; the objective is to connect them to observation-level data

questions.explanation: The framework is explicit: reporting summaries stay, and the objective is to connect them to observation-level data that can be analysed, aggregated and used. What changes is the unit of evidence beneath the summary, not the existence of the summary.

source.title: A New MEAL Approach for CIMMYT

questions.reviewTip: Find the boxed sentence 'Reporting summaries stay' in section 1.

questions.question: A seed systems project in Mexico sets up one registry that breeding, MEAL, the data team and management all draw on, instead of four separate spreadsheets. Which strategic effect does this most directly build?

options.text: Impact
Agility and foresight
Collaboration
Evidence
